articles.headline: Two Hours of Strength Training Per Week Could Add Years to Your Life
articles.body: A major study tracking participants for up to 30 years found that strength training for 90 to 120 minutes per week is the sweet spot for longevity. That level of consistent resistance work was linked to a 19% lower risk of death from cardiovascular disease and a 27% lower risk from neurological disease. The good news: more isn't always better. Researchers found no additional benefit from exceeding 120 minutes weekly, suggesting that moderate, consistent effort beats heroic volume. Combine it with aerobic exercise for even greater protection.
articles.takeaway: Two hours of weekly strength training beats extreme volume. Consistency at moderate intensity is what extends your healthspan.

articles.topic: Hormone fluctuations change exercise perception not ability
articles.headline: Your Hormones Don't Change How Hard You Can Work. Just How It Feels.
articles.body: New research from the University of Oregon rewrites what we thought we knew about female hormones and exercise. Study found that estrogen and progesterone fluctuations across the menstrual cycle don't actually change your ability to exercise hard. What changes is your perception. Women reported workouts felt significantly more difficult when progesterone was high during the luteal phase, but their actual aerobic performance stayed the same. Your power output is consistent. The feeling of effort shifts. Understanding this gap between capability and perceived exertion can help you plan workouts strategically.
articles.takeaway: Hormones shift how hard exercise feels, not what you're actually capable of doing. Work with your perception, not against your ability.

articles.topic: Joint flexibility predicts longevity and independence
articles.headline: Your Flexibility Might Be One of Your Best Longevity Markers
articles.body: A 13-year study following over 3,000 adults found something striking: greater joint flexibility was strongly associated with lower death risk. Researchers tested range of motion at seven sites—ankles, shoulders, knees, spine, wrists, hips, and elbows. The adults who moved better lived longer. The mechanism is clear: flexibility improves mobility, reduces chronic pain, and keeps people active. Without it, people tend to move less, fall more often, and spiral into sedentary patterns. It's not about touching your toes. It's about maintaining the movement freedom to live independently.
articles.takeaway: Flexibility isn't vanity work. It's longevity work. Better movement equals longer life.

articles.topic: Smartwatch hypertension detection FDA approval screening
articles.headline: Your Smartwatch Can Now Flag High Blood Pressure Risks
articles.body: In September 2025, the FDA cleared the Apple Watch Hypertension Notifications feature—a cuffless tool using optical sensors to detect blood flow changes and alert users to potential high blood pressure. The watch doesn't diagnose, but it screens. A new analysis published in JAMA examined what this means at population scale. Samsung watches also offer blood pressure estimates after calibration. While smartwatch readings aren't clinical replacements, they create something valuable: continuous screening that catches what routine doctor visits miss. For busy professionals, it's proactive awareness without extra steps.
articles.takeaway: Smartwatches can now flag hypertension risk. Use them as screening tools, not diagnostic devices, and verify with your doctor.

workout.title: Hip & Ankle Unlock: Deep Opener Flow for Endurance Athletes
workout.tip: Breathe into the deepest point of each stretch for 3–4 full breath cycles; tension releases only when the nervous system feels safe. Never force depth—meet your body where it is today.
workout.warmup: 3 min: 5 slow cat-cow cycles, 10 arm swings, 8 leg swings forward-back each leg, 5 bodyweight squats

exercises.name: 90/90 Hip External Rotation Hold
exercises.notes: Seated, front leg bent at 90° hip and knee, back leg internally rotated. Fold forward gently. This opens the piriformis and addresses glute tightness from running. Common in runners with IT band issues.

exercises.name: Deep Squat Hold with Shoulder Opener
exercises.notes: Feet shoulder-width, sink into a deep squat. On rep 1, interlace hands and pull them over your head. On rep 2, press hands into ground and lift hips slightly higher. Addresses ankle mobility and thoracic extension simultaneously.

exercises.name: Pigeon Pose Progression
exercises.notes: Front leg flexed at 90°, slowly fold forward. If accessible, walk hands forward. Critical for hip external rotators and glute activation. Endurance athletes often have tight outer hips from unilateral leg drive.

exercises.name: Lizard Pose & Hip Flexor Stretch Combo
exercises.reps: 45 sec each side (15 sec lizard, 30 sec hip flexor)
exercises.notes: Lizard: low lunge, forearms on ground, sink hips forward. Follow with rear-foot elevated half-split to hit hip flexors. Essential after running to restore anterior chain length and reduce anterior pelvic tilt.

exercises.name: Supine Spinal Twist with Hip Opening
exercises.notes: Lie supine, one knee to chest then cross body. Keep shoulders flat. This decompresses lumbar spine while opening external hip rotators. Perfect post-brick or post-long-run.

exercises.name: Supported Child's Pose Breathwork
exercises.notes: Forehead on block or pillow, arms extended. Breathe into rib cage and mid-back. Activates parasympathetic nervous system, signals recovery to body. Hold longer than feels necessary.

workout.cooldown: 2 min: gentle neck rolls, 5 shoulder shrugs, conscious breath observation
workout.description: This 40-minute mobility sequence targets hip external rotation, ankle dorsiflexion, and deep squat positioning—restrictions created by repetitive running and cycling. Ideal for marathon and triathlon athletes, this flowing practice restores stride efficiency and reduces compensatory knee stress. Each position is held and breathed into, promoting parasympathetic activation while building functional range.

meal.title: Cottage Cheese & Berries with Granola Crunch
meal.description: High-protein cottage cheese layered with fresh berries and a handful of granola—delivers immediate protein and carbs for muscle repair while being light enough to sit well post-training. It's also dairy-based, which research shows aids recovery.
meal.instructions:
1. Spoon cottage cheese into a bowl.
2. Top with mixed berries (blueberries, strawberries, raspberries—whatever you have).
3. Sprinkle granola over the fruit.
4. Drizzle with a small amount of honey if desired.
meal.tip: Buy pre-portioned berries (frozen or fresh) to eliminate prep. Cottage cheese is a recovery powerhouse and keeps for 2 weeks—stock it in the fridge for grab-and-go meals anytime.
